description: Tina Turner rules Bartertown and the soundtrack of 1985's Mad Max Beyond Thunderdome with this hard-rocking survival anthem, written by Holly Knight and produced by Mike Chapman. It hit No. 15 in the US and won her a Grammy.

pops.text: This is the sound of Bartertown's opening credits: the song plays over the start of Mad Max Beyond Thunderdome, the 1985 film in which Tina Turner stars as Aunty Entity, ruler of Bartertown.
Writer Holly Knight and producer Mike Chapman were a proven Tina team — they'd already co-written 'Better Be Good to Me,' a No. 5 hit from Private Dancer the year before.
Director George Miller wrote the part of Aunty Entity for Turner after seeing her as the Acid Queen in The Who's 1975 film Tommy.
It was recorded in 1985 at Cherokee Studios in Hollywood, with members of the band Device backing Turner — and saxophonist Tim Cappello blowing the solo.
Released on 13 September 1985, this was the soundtrack's second single, following Turner's own 'We Don't Need Another Hero (Thunderdome).'
It climbed to No. 15 on the Billboard Hot 100 and stayed on the chart for 18 weeks — a strong showing in the shadow of 'Hero,' which had gone to No. 2.
DJs liked it even more: the song reached No. 6 on Billboard's Dance chart, while also making No. 41 on the R&B chart.
The official video premiered at the 1985 MTV Awards: Turner strides around with a guitar while clips from the film are cut in around her.
Turner took the song on the road, performing it on her 1985 Private Dancer Tour and on TV shows including Australia's Countdown and the Canadian Juno Awards.
The big payoff came in February 1986: 'One of the Living' won the Grammy for Best Female Rock Vocal Performance — Turner's fifth Grammy overall.

title: One Of The Living

description: Van Morrison's joyful tribute to Fats Domino opens His Band and the Street Choir (1970) with horns and pure R&B energy — and became the highest-charting single of his career, peaking at No. 9 on the Billboard Hot 100.

pops.text: No, it's not about the game: 'Domino' is Van Morrison's personal tribute to New Orleans R&B singer and pianist Fats Domino, a hero of the Belfast radio he grew up on.
Morrison wrote the song years before releasing it — early takes date back to sessions in autumn 1968 at Warners Publishing Studio in New York City.
One theory for the delay: Morrison believed it could be a hit and held it back so it wouldn't fall under a single-release clause in his old Web IV contract.
The released version was cut in spring 1970 at A&R Recording Studios in New York, with Elliot Scheiner engineering.
A flute part was originally written for the song — then dropped for being too complex. The horns that stayed are doing plenty.
It's the opening track of His Band and the Street Choir, Morrison's fourth studio album, released in November 1970, hard on the heels of Moondance.
Warner Bros. had asked Morrison for more radio-friendly hits after Moondance. He delivered: this was the album's first single, released in October 1970.
It peaked at No. 9 on the Billboard Hot 100 — still Morrison's highest-charting single ever, one place above 'Brown Eyed Girl' at No. 10.
Critic Robert Christgau called it a 'superb example of Morrison's loose, allusive white R&B,' while Rolling Stone's Jon Landau singled out the guitar intro for praise.
Critic Dave Marsh ranked 'Domino' at No. 197 in his 1989 book The Heart of Rock and Soul: The 1001 Greatest Singles Ever Made.

title: Domino

description: A lovesick plea from Violent Femmes' 1983 debut, built on Gordon Gano's pleading vocal and Brian Ritchie's roaming acoustic bass — complete with one of rock's rare unaccompanied bass solos and a happily unconvincing reggae groove.

pops.text: Track three on the Femmes' 1983 debut, this is the album's breather — arriving right after the twin jolts of 'Blister in the Sun' and 'Kiss Off.'
Gordon Gano wrote most of the debut while he was still in high school in Wisconsin. He was only 18 when the band recorded the album in July 1982.

The band had been discovered the previous summer, busking outside Milwaukee's Oriental Theatre, when the Pretenders' James Honeyman-Scott heard them and Chrissie Hynde invited them to play a set that night.
Producer Mark Van Hecke recorded the album for Slash Records, the Los Angeles punk label. It was released on 13 April 1983.
Brian Ritchie calls the groove 'so inauthentic, and not really reggae — it just refers to reggae. An oblique reference.' Punk does reggae, approximately.
The famous break wasn't planned. Ritchie recalls the band reaching a point where 'something better start happening' — nobody knew what, so he started playing a bass solo.
The result is one of rock's rare unaccompanied bass solos: just Ritchie's acoustic bass guitar carrying the whole song by itself.
That little girl peering through a window on the album cover? Three-year-old Billie Jo Campbell, spotted walking down a California street and paid $100 for the photograph.
The debut was a word-of-mouth phenomenon: in 1987 it went gold without ever having appeared on the Billboard 200 — a unique feat at the time.
It finally went platinum on 1 February 1991, eight years after release — and only then did the album chart at all, peaking at No. 171. A 2023 deluxe reissue even added a demo of this song.

title: Please Do Not Go

description: A two-minute-and-change instrumental strut from Vulfpeck's 2013 EP My First Car. No lyrics, no chorus — just Wurlitzer, drums, bass and guitar, and a groove built for exactly what the title says: walking very fast, with purpose.

pops.text: An instrumental with a mission statement for a title: 'The Speedwalker' comes from Vulfpeck's third EP, My First Car, released in 2013 on the band's own Vulf Records.
It's short and built to move — just 2 minutes 28 seconds of Wurlitzer, drums, bass and guitar, with not a single lyric.
Vulfpeck formed in 2011 at the University of Michigan's music school, where Jack Stratton, Theo Katzman, Woody Goss and Joe Dart met as students.

Stratton conceived the band as an imaginary German version of the great American session bands — the Funk Brothers, the Wrecking Crew, Muscle Shoals — after reading an interview with producer Reinhold Mack.
The band was YouTube-first from day one: their debut track 'Beastly' arrived as a YouTube video in April 2011, before any EP existed.
My First Car was a small landmark for the band: its track 'Wait for the Moment,' sung by Antwaun Stanley, was the first Vulfpeck song ever to feature a vocal.
The official video's credits are very Vulf: 'Jack Stratton — wurli, composer, walker. Theo Katzman — drums.' Yes, 'walker' is an official credit.
The video didn't appear until December 2016, three years after the EP — and it simply shows Stratton strutting and speedwalking, exactly as advertised.
A year after My First Car, the band released Sleepify, an album of complete silence on Spotify; its streaming royalties funded an admission-free tour.
Everything here is in-house: Vulfpeck release their music themselves on Vulf Records, building a worldwide following largely through low-budget performance videos like this one.

title: The Speedwalker

description: Paul McCartney goes disco — with a flamenco guitar break — on this 1979 Wings single. Begun as a solo recording in 1978, it reached No. 5 in both the US and UK and went gold in America.

pops.text: McCartney has said he wrote this after a night at a disco, deliberately setting out to make a dance record — then added a spirited flamenco guitar break for good measure.
It began on 6 February 1978 as an instrumental backing track McCartney recorded by himself at Rude Studio in Campbeltown, Scotland.
The groove runs on a Roland CR-78 drum machine — the same machine Blondie used on 'Heart of Glass.'

A year later Wings needed a single to accompany Back to the Egg, so Paul pulled the track out and the full band finished it: Denny Laine and Laurence Juber mirroring his guitar parts, Steve Holley adding percussion.
Released on 23 March 1979 as a standalone single, it never appeared on a Wings studio album. In the US it was McCartney's first single under his new deal with Columbia Records.
The band's full take ran over seven minutes: the 7-inch single edited it to 4:15, while the complete 7:14 version went out on the 12-inch single.
The music video shows Wings performing in 1930s costumes. Stills from the video were used on the single's sleeve.
It reached No. 5 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 5 on the UK Singles Chart in the spring of 1979 — a transatlantic matching pair.
The single was certified gold by the RIAA for sales of over one million copies in the United States.
John Lennon's review was pure Lennon: he said he did not care for the song, but he enjoyed McCartney's bass guitar on it. The B-side was 'Daytime Nighttime Suffering.'

title: Goodnight Tonight

description: The nearly eight-minute lead single from Wooden Shjips' 2018 album V, written by Ripley Johnson on a Portland porch while wildfire ash fell like snow and the sun glowed through the haze.

pops.text: Track five on V, Wooden Shjips' fifth album, released May 25, 2018 on Thrill Jockey. Yes, the band name is pronounced simply 'ships.'
This was the album's first single — and at almost eight minutes, it was in no hurry. Psych-rock does not do three-minute pop edits.
Ripley Johnson wrote it in the summer of 2017, watching wildfires ravage the Pacific Northwest. He described ash snowing down on Portland.
The eerie gift of that smoke: ash in the atmosphere dimmed the sun enough that Johnson could sit on his porch and literally stare at it, a ball of fire.
That same summer brought the 2017 solar eclipse, which also worked its way into the song. Apocalyptic skies, meet blissed-out groove.
The quartet: Johnson on guitar and vocals, Dusty Jermier on bass, Omar Ahsanuddin on drums and Nash Whalen on organ and keys.
V was the band's first album in five years, following 2013's Back to Land. Half the band still lived in San Francisco, Johnson in Portland.
The basics were tracked by Jason Powers at Types Foundry Studio in Portland, with guitars and vocals largely recorded in Johnson's home studio.
Johnson wrote V's songs as an antidote to political and natural anxiety. The title V is the two-finger peace sign — peace, beauty and resistance.
Johnson splits his time with Moon Duo, the side project he formed in 2009 with Sanae Yamada. One singer, two hypnotic bands.

title: Staring At The Sun

description: A No. 1 R&B and dance hit from Conscious Party (1988), the Grammy-winning breakthrough by Bob and Rita Marley's children, polished to a pop shine by Talking Heads' rhythm section.

pops.text: Track five on Conscious Party, released April 5, 1988 on Virgin. It was Ziggy Marley and the Melody Makers' third album — and their breakthrough.
The Melody Makers were four of Bob and Rita Marley's children: Ziggy, Stephen, Sharon and Cedella. The family band was formed back in 1979.
Ziggy co-wrote this one with Tyrone Downie. Ziggy wrote nearly everything else on the album himself.
Producers? Chris Frantz and Tina Weymouth — the Talking Heads and Tom Tom Club rhythm section, who gave the record its electro-pop sheen.
It was recorded at Sigma Sound in New York City, the legendary studio behind countless Philadelphia soul classics.
As a single, 'Tumblin' Down' hit No. 1 on both the Hot R&B Singles chart and the Hot Dance Music/Maxi-Singles Sales chart.
It crossed over, too: No. 5 on Billboard's Modern Rock Tracks. A reggae single climbing the rock chart in 1988 was no small trick.
Conscious Party peaked at No. 23 on the Billboard 200 and was certified platinum in the US — a million copies for the Marley kids.
The album won the Grammy for Best Reggae Album in 1989, the group's first of three career Grammy wins as the Melody Makers.
The guest list was stacked: Keith Richards played lead guitar on the album's 'Lee and Molly,' and Talking Heads bandmate Jerry Harrison played Hammond organ.

title: Tumblin' Down

description: Half Moon Run's contribution to producer Connor Seidel's 1969 project — original Canadian songs recorded in the style of late-'60s folk, cut live off the floor with strings and harmonica.

pops.text: Released as a single on March 10, 2022, ahead of the album 1969, which followed on April 12. A 2022 song with its heart in another era entirely.
The 1969 Collective was producer Connor Seidel's idea: invite a roster of artists to each contribute an original song recorded in the style of late-'60s folk.
Careful with the Connors: the producer is Connor Seidel, while Half Moon Run's guitarist is Conner Molander. Different men, one letter apart.
Half Moon Run remember this song coming together unusually fast. They recorded it live off the floor, everyone playing together in the room.
Hear the period detail: the drums are hard-panned into the right ear, a nod to early Bob Dylan records, leaving space for the band's three-part harmonies.
The arrangement is led by strings duetting with harmonica — a new musical setting for a band better known for layered percussion and indie rock.
The band's own review of the brief: 'Late '60s is an aesthetic that we chase.' Mission understood, mission accomplished.
Half Moon Run are a Montreal trio — Devon Portielje, Dylan Phillips and Conner Molander — formed in the Mile End neighbourhood in 2009.
The 1969 album's lineup is a Canadian who's-who: Elisapie, Safia Nolin, Ariane Moffatt, Louis-Jean Cormier, Les Soeurs Boulay and Matt Holubowski among others.
The collaboration stuck: Seidel went on to produce Half Moon Run's 2023 album Salt, mostly made at his Treehouse Studio north of Montreal.

title: Fatal Line

description: Addison Groove Project's signature cover — a Boston jam-funk sextet, formed by Wellesley high schoolers, tearing into Alan Hawkshaw's 1968 Hammond-organ nugget for the Mohawks.

pops.text: This is a cover, and the band never hid it: written by Alan Hawkshaw, it first appeared on The Champ, the 1968 album by his studio band the Mohawks.
The Mohawks were crack British session musicians assembled by Hawkshaw, a Hammond organ exponent. The Champ later became a crate-digger and hip-hop sampling favourite.
Hawkshaw went on to write some of Britain's most-heard TV themes, including Countdown, Grange Hill and Channel 4 News. From funk obscurity to teatime television.
Addison Groove Project formed in 1997, made up of five Wellesley, Massachusetts high school seniors cutting their teeth on Kool & the Gang covers.
The lineup grew to a sextet: Brendan McGinn on guitar, John Hall on bass, Andrew Keith on drums, Rob Marscher on keys, and Dave Adams and Ben Groppe on saxes.
Their live album Wicked Live was recorded in Saratoga Springs, New York, on September 15, 2000 — this tune was part of that era's signature set.
A 2002 New York review caught the ritual: the band took the stage at 12:35 a.m. and opened with this song, 'much to the crowd's delight.'
One Charleston reviewer dubbed keyboardist Rob Marscher a 'junior Medeski' — high praise in jam-band land, after John Medeski of Medeski Martin & Wood.
Marscher later played with reggae star Matisyahu, while saxophonist Dave Adams went into teaching music in the Milton, Massachusetts public schools.
Signature-cover status, confirmed: when the reunited band played Brooklyn Bowl in 2013, this song was the encore that brought the evening to a close.

title: Beat Me 'Til I'm Blue

description: The title track of Canadian producer Greg Vickers' 2012 comeback EP — breaks, groovy organ and Rhodes, and a saxophone that dissolves into feedback before the groove snaps back.

pops.text: Title track of the Soul Sugar EP, released August 20, 2012 on Timewarp Music — the first new Afternoons In Stereo material in over two years.
Afternoons In Stereo is one man: Canadian producer Greg Vickers, who fuses analog sensibilities with digital production — vintage and modern at once.
The label is a journey in itself: Timewarp Music is based in Athens, Greece. A Canadian producer, a Greek label, a worldwide lounge scene.
The sound, per the label: breaks-driven, with groovy organ and lush Rhodes keys rising to the centre of the track. Sweet, as advertised.
Then the twist: the saxophone descends into a shudder of feedback and distortion before the song returns to its addictive groove.
The four-track EP paired it with 'Driving To Montenegro' and 'Blow,' plus a Mr. Confuse remix of 'Driving To Montenegro.'
Everything was mastered by Angelos Timewarp Stoumpos, the label's founder. The boss's ears were the final stop for every Timewarp release.
The song graduated: it became the lead single of the fifth Afternoons In Stereo album, simply titled 5, released in 2013, where it sits as track four.
Its kitschy retro video became a genuine underground hit on YouTube, and the song was licensed for multiple media projects and platforms.
It even got its own remix EP in March 2013, with new versions by Niles Philips, AUditors DOmination, Leon and Zamali — four takes on the sweetness.

title: Soul Sugar

description: A Dutch afro-funk groove from Afro Soul System, built by DJ/producer Phil Martin and Ton van der Kolk's AIFF — Fela Kuti-inspired horns, percussion and guitar melted with deep funk, soul and jazz.

pops.text: AIFF unpacks to Afro Influenced Funk Federation. The Dutch crew built its own version of afro-funk around DJ and producer Phil Martin and musician Ton van der Kolk.
This is a track from Afro Soul System, released September 5, 2007 on Social Beats. Shazam's credits list A.C. van der Kolk and T. van der Holst as its composers.
The stated influence is right up front: classic afro-funk, above all Fela Kuti. The label says AIFF set out to bring afro-funk 'to a new dimension.'
The recipe is a melt, not a copy: the label lists their favourite styles as deep-funk, soul and jazz, plus reggae and afro music, all folded into one sound.
AIFF played most instruments themselves. For vocals and horns they simply called friends they liked working with — including Marco Hijl on saxophone and flute.
Before the album came a limited first 7-inch, 'Akwaaba' / 'Watergirls.' It was highly recommended by Paul Murphy of Afroart Recordings and Andy Smith of Portishead.
That little 7-inch travelled: international DJs Keb Darge and Snowboy played it at their gigs, and the label notes that even Paul Weller loved the tune.
The single did its job — the positive response to 'Akwaaba' is what made AIFF decide to come up with a full album, Afro Soul System.

The album around this track is a guest party: Crucial T, formerly of ska group The Continentals, appears on 'Afro Riddim,' Jazzinvaders singer Linda Bloemhard sings 'Life,' and Travis Blaque raps on 'Ugly Duckling.'
The label placed AIFF alongside Quantic, The New Mastersounds and Speedometer, and name-checked the Daktaris and the Budos Band as contemporary favourites. Shazam clocks this groove at 123 BPM.

title: The Seduction

description: Al Green's silken pledge of devotion, written in minutes and argued over for days — his only Hot 100 No. 1, a National Recording Registry pick, and soul's definitive wedding-and-everything song.

pops.text: Producer Willie Mitchell and drummer Al Jackson Jr. handed Green a rough mix of a tune they had developed — and Green wrote the lyrics in about five minutes.
Then came the fight: Green didn't want to record it, and argued with Mitchell for two days before finally agreeing to cut the song that defined him.
It was produced and recorded by Willie Mitchell and mixed by Mitchell and Terry Manning for Hi Records. The writers are Green, Mitchell and Al Jackson Jr.
Released as a single in November 1971, it became the title track of Green's 1972 album Let's Stay Together. The original B-side was 'Tomorrow's Dream.'
Chart report: No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in February 1972, 16 weeks on the chart, and nine weeks atop the R&B chart. Billboard ranked it the No. 11 song of 1972.
For all his hits, this remains Al Green's only No. 1 single on the Hot 100 — the signature song of the great Memphis soul voice.
Rolling Stone ranked it 60th on its 2004 list of the 500 Greatest Songs of All Time. In 1999 the recording was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame.
The Library of Congress selected it in 2010 for the National Recording Registry, its annual list of recordings that are culturally and historically significant.
Tina Turner's 1983 cover was her comeback single: No. 6 in the UK — one place higher than Green's original — No. 26 in the US, No. 1 on the US Dance chart, and a place on Private Dancer.

Two famous afterlives: Quentin Tarantino used it in Pulp Fiction (1994), and on January 19, 2012 President Barack Obama sang a phrase of it at the Apollo Theater — sales of Green's recording jumped 490% the following week.

title: Let's Stay Together

description: Jerry Cantrell's ode to Mother Love Bone's Andrew Wood, launched on the Singles soundtrack before anchoring Dirt. Cantrell sings the verses, Layne Staley detonates the chorus.

pops.text: Jerry Cantrell wrote this as a tribute to his friend Andrew Wood, lead singer of Mother Love Bone, who died of a heroin overdose in 1990.
Cantrell explained in the Music Bank liner notes that it was also aimed at people who judge: 'I always hate people who judge the decisions others make.'
Listen to the handoff: Cantrell sings the verses, while Layne Staley sings the chorus. That two-voice tension became the band's signature.
It first appeared on the soundtrack to Cameron Crowe's 1992 film Singles — where the members of Alice in Chains make a cameo appearance as a bar band.
Columbia serviced it to US radio on June 8, 1992. Months later it landed on the band's second album, Dirt, released September 29, 1992.
The song was produced by Alice in Chains with Rick Parashar, and runs a tight 3:27 — no wasted motion anywhere in it.
Chart report: No. 31 on Billboard's Mainstream Rock Tracks in 1992, then No. 19 in the UK in January 1993 — at the time the band's highest-charting song there.
The video was co-directed by Cameron Crowe and Josh Taft, and it won Best Video from a Film at the 1993 MTV Video Music Awards.
The honours kept coming: VH1 named it the 88th Best Hard Rock Song of All Time in 2009, and Paste ranked it No. 3 on its 50 Best Grunge Songs list in 2014.
In January 2019 it soundtracked the trailer for season 2 of Netflix's The Punisher — and promptly peaked at No. 15 on Billboard's Hot Rock Songs chart, 27 years after release.

title: Would?

description: Dickey Betts' jazz-tinged instrumental from Idlewild South — named for a Macon gravestone to hide the woman it was really about, and later stretched into a Fillmore East legend.

pops.text: No singer, no problem: this is an instrumental, written by guitarist Dickey Betts. It was the first instrumental written by a member of the band.
It's the fourth track on Idlewild South, the band's second album, released September 23, 1970 on Capricorn Records and produced by Tom Dowd. The studio version runs 6:54.
The title is a disguise. Betts named it after a headstone he saw for Elizabeth Jones Reed Napier in Rose Hill Cemetery in the band's hometown of Macon, Georgia.
The real subject was a woman Betts was involved with in Macon — who happened to be the girlfriend of musician Boz Scaggs. The gravestone name cloaked her identity.
Rose Hill was the band's hangout — members went there in their early days to relax and write songs. It later became the final resting place of Duane and Gregg Allman, Berry Oakley and Butch Trucks.

The jazz in this rock band is deliberate: Duane Allman said of Miles Davis' Kind of Blue, 'I've listened to that album so many times that for the past couple of years, I haven't hardly listened to anything else.'

Rolling Stone's original Idlewild South review said the piece 'just goes and goes for a stupendous, and unnoticed, seven minutes.' The Album Guide later called the studio take 'the blueprint of a concert warhorse.'
This is the studio original — but the 13:04 version on 1971's At Fillmore East, from the March 13, 1971 first show, is generally considered the definitive rendition.
On stage it kept growing: concert performances sometimes ran half an hour or more. Rolling Stone named it one of its Fifty Best Songs Over Seven Minutes Long in 2007.
Jazz flautist Herbie Mann loved it enough to record it twice — on Push Push (1971), with Duane Allman on guitar, and again on Turtle Bay (1973).

title: In Memory Of Elizabeth Reed

description: The San Diego trio's escapist 2025 single, launched with a camp spy-thriller video in which L.O.S.T. stands for League of Operatives for Strategic Treachery. Getting lost, on purpose.

pops.text: San Diego indie-pop trio almost monday — Dawson Daugherty on vocals, Cole Clisby on guitar and Luke Fabry on bass — released 'lost' as a single on October 3, 2025, on Hollywood Records.
It was written by all three band members with Simon Oscroft. The band calls it a song about escapism and finding yourself by leaving what you know behind.
The band started in a San Diego surf shop, according to Disney Music Publishing — three friends shaping a sound that feels coastal without feeling cliché.
Name check: they initially wanted to call themselves The Mondays, but the name was taken. Almost Monday was the alternative they settled on.
The video, directed by longtime collaborator Sam Kristofski, is a Bourne movie bent toward B-movie camp — globe-trotting, shaky surveillance and crowd chases included.
In the clip the trio play absurd alter egos: Jean-Luc Sage as Dream Weaver, Coleman Rice as Big Data and Darwin Herty as Chicken Bone, exchanging a very mysterious black bag.
The video bills itself as an adaptation of the spy novel Deep State by J.J. Clark — a book that does not exist. It also expands the title: L.O.S.T., League of Operatives for Strategic Treachery.
Timing: the single arrived after the band's sold-out debut headline tour across the US and Europe, and a summer of festivals including Outside Lands, Pinkpop and Lollapalooza Paris.
Days after release they hit the road again, joining The Band CAMINO on the NeverAlways Tour, kicking off October 10 in Atlanta and heading to Brooklyn, Los Angeles and Nashville.
The afterlife came fast: 'lost' reached No. 40 on Billboard's Alternative Airplay chart, and at the 2026 San Diego Music Awards it was nominated for Song of the Year.

title: lost
